messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
We need about 2,500 feet, and the flight time window is 185-195 s. Motors are limited to G or smaller. Show me what you've got.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 2,500 ft. 2500 * 0.3048 = 762 m, so the band is 762 m ±5% (about 724 to 800 m). Flight time is a hard window of 185 to 195 s, not a loose "about". Motor class is at most G. Nothing is said about rail, wind, or landing speed, so I assume a 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, and a 6 m/s maximum touchdown. Single stage, straight up, sea level.
2. Feasibility: a drag-free burnout speed for 762 m is sqrt(2*9.81*762) = 122 m/s. A real model rocket gives up a large share of that to drag, so the impulse has to sit in the E to F range; a full G on a light airframe would sail well past 800 m. I need the catalog numbers before choosing.

2. Feasibility: D12 is 16.8 N*s, E12 is 27.1 N*s at 11.2 N for 2.41 s, E9 is 27.9 N*s but only 9.2 N average, F15 is 49.6 N*s, and the G80 lookup came back as a G80T at 135.6 N*s. Ratios to the E12 are 16.8 / 27.1 = 0.62, 49.6 / 27.1 = 1.83, and 135.6 / 27.1 = 5.0. The D is likely short of 724 m, the F and G are likely past 800 m on a light rocket, and the E9's lower thrust is worse off a 1.5 m rail. E12 stays inside the G cap and is the closest impulse. Its longest delay is 8 s; burn plus that delay is only about 10 s, which is early for a coast to 762 m, so the chute will be an apogee event on a plugged motor rather than motor ejection.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.12 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 11.2 / (0.12 * 9.81) = 9.5. Weight is 0.12 * 9.81 = 1.18 N, so rail acceleration is (11.2 - 1.18) / 0.12 = 83.5 m/s^2 and rail exit is sqrt(2 * 83.5 * 1.5) = 15.8 m/s, just above 15 m/s before counting the thrust spike. Propellant is about 0.036 kg, so descent mass is 0.12 - 0.036 = 0.084 kg. Time to apogee is a guess of 12 s, leaving 190 - 12 = 178 s of descent, so the sink rate for 762 m is 762 / 178 = 4.28 m/s. Canopy area at Cd 0.8 is 2 * 0.084 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.3^2) = 0.091 m^2, and the diameter is sqrt(4 * 0.091 / 3.1416) = 0.34 m. I'll fit a 0.36 m chute so the landing sits under 6 m/s with a little margin.
4. Draft: 33.7 mm cardboard body, 0.55 m long, ogive nose, three balsa fins, 24 mm mount, Estes E12 plugged, 0.36 m ripstop chute at apogee. Checking that draft.

messages.name: simulate
messages.content: {"ok": false, "error": "invalid design: motor E12 is 24 mm but the motor_mount inner diameter is 23.8 mm"}

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulate call failed before any flight numbers. The mount inner diameter is 0.0248 - 2 * 0.0005 = 0.0238 m, which is 23.8 mm, and the motor is 24 mm. Nothing else can be scored until the motor fits.
5. Fix: the failing fit is 23.8 mm against 24 mm. I'll raise the mount outer diameter from 0.0248 m to 0.0254 m and leave the 0.0005 m wall, so the inner diameter becomes 0.0254 - 2 * 0.0005 = 0.0244 m (24.4 mm). The body inner diameter is still larger than 0.0254 m, so the mount still fits the tube. Same airframe, same chute, same motor.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 501.0 m. The goal is 762 m within 5%, so 724 to 800 m, and 501.0 / 762 = 0.66, a miss. Flight time is 131.6 s against the 185 to 195 s window, also a miss. The short flight follows the low apogee: descent is about 131.6 - 8.53 = 123 s from 501 m. Gates that pass: rail exit 23.1 m/s (above 15), thrust-to-weight 9.6 (above 3), margin 2.36 cal (above 1), landing 4.0 m/s (under 6). Liftoff mass 0.119 kg matches the 0.12 kg guess. Motor is an E, inside the G limit.
5. Fix: apogee is the cause, and the flight-time miss comes with it. The F15 has 49.6 N*s against the E12's 27.1 N*s (49.6 / 27.1 = 1.83) and still sits under a G. It is a 29 mm motor, so the mount has to grow with it: outer diameter 0.0304 m, wall 0.0005 m, inner diameter 0.0304 - 2 * 0.0005 = 0.0294 m, length 0.12 m. Body, fins, and the 0.36 m chute stay put. Added motor mass is about 0.103 - 0.060 = 0.043 kg, so liftoff near 0.119 + 0.043 = 0.162 kg and thrust-to-weight near 14.5 / (0.162 * 9.81) = 9.1.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 743.6 m. Against 762 m that is (762 - 743.6) / 762 = 2.4% low, inside the 5% band, so altitude passes. Flight time 173.8 s is short of the 185 s floor by 185 - 173.8 = 11.2 s, so the window fails. Stability at rail exit is 0.86 cal, under the 1.0 cal minimum, so that gate fails too. The heavier 29 mm motor pulled the margin down. Rail exit 15.5 m/s still clears 15, thrust-to-weight is 9.1, and landing is 4.5 m/s under 6. Motor is an F, inside the G limit.
5. Fix: two misses, one cause each. Margin is 0.86 cal because the fins are small for the aft mass, so I am going from 3 fins to 4 and stretching the span from 0.055 m to 0.07 m, with the root trailing edge moved to the aft end. Flight time is the chute: descent took 173.8 - 10.4 = 163.4 s, and 190 - 10.4 = 179.6 s would land in the window. That sink rate is 743.6 / 179.6 = 4.14 m/s against the 4.5 m/s landing, so the diameter goes to 0.36 * 4.5 / 4.14 = 0.39 m. I'll fit a 0.40 m chute. Motor, body, and nose stay the same so the altitude that just passed is left alone.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 666.4 m. That is (762 - 666.4) / 762 = 12.5% under 762 m, outside the 5% band, so altitude now fails. Flight time 168.1 s is still short of 185 s by 185 - 168.1 = 16.9 s. The fin growth did what was asked of the margin: 2.13 cal at rail exit, above 1.0, and the burn stays at 2.13. Rail exit 15.9 m/s, thrust-to-weight 8.8, landing 4.2 m/s, all clear. The altitude that used to pass was 743.6 m, and 743.6 - 666.4 = 77.2 m of that went away with the extra fin area.
5. Fix: the drag of the larger fins is the new miss, so those fins go back to the set that held 743.6 m (3 fins, span 0.055 m) and the margin comes from 5 g in the nose instead. That keeps the CP where it was and shifts the CG forward, which is the 0.14 cal the earlier 0.86 cal result was short. The chute stays at 0.40 m so the descent from about 740 m can fill the 185 to 195 s window. Checking the margin of that combination before flying it.

4. Check: stability puts the static margin at 2.06 cal on a 0.169 kg liftoff, CG at 0.484 m and CP at 0.554 m. That is above the 1.0 cal launch minimum, with room for the rail-exit number to come out a bit lower than the static value. The 5 g nose weight is enough, so the design does not change. Flying it next.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 744.5 m. Against 762 m that is (762 - 744.5) / 762 = 2.3% low, inside the 5% band. Flight time 186.5 s sits in the 185 to 195 s window, 186.5 - 185 = 1.5 s above the floor. Rail exit 15.8 m/s clears 15, thrust-to-weight is 8.7, rail-exit margin is 1.3 cal (the static figure was 2.06), burn margin stays 1.3 cal, and landing is 4.2 m/s under 6. The F15 is inside the G limit. Every check passes.
5. Fix: no further change; this flight meets the altitude window, the time window, and the safety gates.
6. Uncertainty: 186.5 s is only 1.5 s inside the window, and the chute Cd of 0.8 is a model value. A real canopy that sank at 4.5 m/s instead of 4.2 m/s would scale that time to about 186.5 * 4.2 / 4.5 = 174 s and miss the floor. Rail exit at 15.8 m/s is 0.8 m/s above the gate, so a heavier build can fail the rail even if the altitude still looks fine. Drag and the 0.169 kg mass are model numbers; weigh the finished rocket.

F15 in a 33.7 mm cardboard airframe, 0.67 m long, with 5 g of nose weight and a 0.40 m chute opening at apogee.
The flight is 744.5 m (744.5 / 0.3048 = 2440 ft) and 186.5 s, with a 4.2 m/s landing.
Rail exit is 15.8 m/s at 1.3 cal. The time window only has 1.5 s to spare.
